strings.name: Maia Sandu
strings.role: President of Moldova and former prime minister
strings.summary: Maia Sandu entered politics from economics and public administration, serving as education minister and prime minister before becoming Moldova’s first woman president in 2020. She began a second term in 2024. She advocates anti-corruption measures, institutional reform and EU membership, amid continuing debate over judicial independence, electoral competition and foreign interference.
strings.coverageNote: Information checked through 18 November 2026, with recent activity supported by reporting on her 16 November Brussels meeting. Elections and inaugurations, party and state offices, EU candidacy and membership, and observers’ assessments and judicial rulings are distinguished.
strings.influence.rationale: She advances Moldova’s anti-corruption and European integration agenda; her political work relates to Eastern European security and institutional reform.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in Risipeni on 24 May 1972. She graduated in management from Moldova’s Academy of Economic Studies in 1994, earned a master’s in international relations in 1998, and obtained Harvard Kennedy School’s Mid-Career Master in Public Administration (MC/MPA) in 2010, not a Master in Public Policy (MPP).
strings.facts.f2.label: Economics and development work
strings.facts.f2.value: She worked in the economy ministry and the World Bank’s Chișinău office, then advised a World Bank executive director in Washington from June 2010 to July 2012. Being an adviser was distinct from serving as executive director or World Bank president.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Stages of European integration
strings.highlights.h1.text: She made European integration a central political objective. Moldova obtained candidate status and advanced negotiations but must still complete reforms and accession procedures. The goal voiced in 2026 of concluding talks by early 2028 was an ambition, not completed membership.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Election assessments and institutional accountability
strings.highlights.h2.text: OSCE/ODIHR found the 2024 elections well administered and candidates able to campaign freely, while noting favourable media coverage for the incumbent and intertwined presidential and referendum campaigns that denied fully equal opportunities. This assessment is distinct from the Constitutional Court’s confirmation of the results.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Takes the oath for a second presidential term
strings.timeline.t1.text: She was sworn in again after defeating Alexandr Stoianoglo in the 3 November runoff. Her final total was 930,139 votes, or 55.35%. The runoff, validation of the result and December inauguration occurred on different dates.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Moldova formally opens EU accession negotiations
strings.timeline.t2.text: The EU and Moldova held their first accession intergovernmental conference. The 2023 political decision, 2024 negotiating-framework approval and formal opening were separate steps. Prime Minister Dorin Recean led Moldova’s delegation; this was not Sandu personally signing an accession treaty.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Moldova receives EU candidate status
strings.timeline.t3.text: The European Council took the decision. Candidacy was a step in the country’s accession process, not EU membership or confirmation that every reform requirement had been fulfilled.
strings.timeline.t4.title: First takes office as Moldova’s president
strings.timeline.t4.text: She was sworn in after defeating Igor Dodon in the 15 November runoff, becoming Moldova’s first woman president. She resigned as Action and Solidarity Party chair that December; the head-of-state and party-chair roles are separate.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Cabinet loses a no-confidence vote
strings.timeline.t5.text: A dispute over selecting the prosecutor general fractured the coalition; 63 members of the 101-seat parliament supported dismissal. Ion Chicu’s government was sworn in on 14 November. The no-confidence vote and the successor’s inauguration were separate events.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Becomes prime minister of a coalition government
strings.timeline.t6.text: She formed a government based on cooperation between the ACUM alliance and the Socialists, serving for about five months. As prime minister she headed the government; Dodon remained president. This service was separate from her later presidential terms.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Action and Solidarity Party holds founding congress
strings.timeline.t7.text: The party grew from a political movement launched in December 2015, with Sandu becoming its chair. The Justice Ministry registered it on 26 May. The initiative’s launch, founding congress and legal registration had distinct dates.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Becomes education minister
strings.timeline.t8.text: She returned home after her World Bank advisory work in Washington and served as education minister until July 2015. Education reform was an early part of her political career; it does not establish that corruption had been eliminated.
